Healthy.name: Healthy Sugarcane
Healthy.description: The leaf and stalk display healthy physiological characteristics with uniform green coloration, intact venation, and no signs of chlorosis, fungal pustules, or vascular discoloration.
symptoms: Vibrant, uniform green leaf blades and midribs
Smooth stalk epidermis without internal or external reddening
Active vegetative growth with normal tillering and leaf unfurling
No necrotic spots, water-soaked lesions, or mosaic mottling
causes: Optimal soil nutrition (balanced N-P-K and micronutrients)
Adequate irrigation and well-drained root zone
Effective weed and borer pest control
Use of certified disease-free seed setts
management: Maintain regular field monitoring and scouting schedules
Ensure balanced fertilization according to soil test recommendations
Maintain clean cultivation and sanitize field harvesting equipment
prevention: Plant certified high-yielding resistant or tolerant varieties
Employ crop rotation with legumes or green manure crops
Ensure proper row spacing (1.2 to 1.5 m) for aeration and sunlight penetration
Healthy.when_to_seek_help: Continue standard agronomic practices. If unexpected leaf discoloration, wilting, or lesions emerge during the monsoon or tillering stage, consult a local extension specialist.

RedRot.name: Red Rot Disease
RedRot.description: Known as the 'cancer of sugarcane', Red Rot is the most devastating fungal disease of sugarcane. It infects both the internal stalk vascular system and the leaf midribs, leading to catastrophic sucrose inversion, stem rotting, and crop lodging.
symptoms: Internal stalk reddening with diagnostic transverse white patches across the pith
Dark red or reddish-brown lesions with straw-colored centers along the leaf midrib
Alcoholic or acidic fermentation odor when affected canes are split open
Sudden yellowing, drying, and downward drooping of top spindle leaves from margins inward
causes: Seed sett transmission through infected planting material
Fungal conidia carried by irrigation water, rain splash, and wind
Pathogen entry through root primordia, growth cracks, or stalk borer tunneling wounds
Waterlogged soil conditions and high humidity (above 80%)
management: Immediately uproot and incinerate all infected stools to prevent pathogen sporulation
Drain standing water immediately from infected field zones
Avoid ratooning heavily infected sugarcane fields
Disinfect cutting knives and implements with 10% sodium hypochlorite between rows
Apply approved protective fungicides (such as carbendazim or thiophanate-methyl) strictly following registered agricultural label specifications
prevention: Plant certified disease-resistant sugarcane varieties (e.g., Co 0238 substitutes or local resistant clones)
Treat seed setts with Moist Hot Air Treatment (MHAT at 54°C for 2.5 hours) or fungicide sett dipping before planting
Adopt a minimum 2-year crop rotation with paddy, maize, or leguminous crops
Avoid flood irrigation from diseased fields to healthy plots
RedRot.when_to_seek_help: Contact your district agricultural officer or research station immediately upon detecting split-stalk reddening or clump wilting, as Red Rot can rapidly spread to adjacent farms.

Rust.name: Sugarcane Rust
Rust.pathogen: Puccinia melanocephala (Common Rust) / Puccinia kuehnii (Orange Rust)
Rust.description: Sugarcane rust is a foliar fungal disease causing widespread chlorotic flecks that rupture into powdery brown pustules, drastically reducing photosynthetic area and tonnage.
symptoms: Tiny, elongated yellowish or chlorotic flecks on both leaf surfaces
Flecks expand into reddish-brown or orange pustules (uredinia) parallel to leaf veins
Ruptured pustules release clouds of powdery orange-brown fungal spores upon touch
Severe infections cause leaves to curl, scorch, and prematurely desiccate, resembling frost burn
causes: Airborne urediniospores carried over long distances by wind currents
Extended leaf wetness (dew or light rain for 8-12 continuous hours)
Moderate temperatures (18°C to 28°C) paired with high relative humidity (>85%)
Dense canopy microclimate restricting airflow
management: Strip and safely dispose of heavily infected bottom canopy leaves during early infestation
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that lengthens leaf moisture duration
Apply labeled agricultural fungicides (e.g., azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, or mancozeb) according to official local extension dosages if disease pressure crosses economic threshold
prevention: Select and cultivate rust-resistant sugarcane varieties suited to your agro-climatic zone
Optimize planting density to promote wind circulation and faster canopy drying
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization, which creates succulent tissue highly susceptible to rust fungi
Balance soil nutrition with adequate potassium (potash) to strengthen plant cell walls
Rust.when_to_seek_help: Seek professional diagnosis if orange pustules appear on young crops under 4 months old or if pustules cover more than 30% of the upper canopy foliage.

Mosaic.name: Sugarcane Mosaic
Mosaic.pathogen: Sugarcane Mosaic Virus (SCMV) / Sorghum Mosaic Virus
Mosaic.description: A systemic viral infection causing distinctive mosaic patterns of contrasting dark and light green patches on leaves, stunting tillers, and depressing cane yield and sugar extraction.
symptoms: Irregular patches of pale green, yellowish, or chlorotic islands contrasting against normal dark green leaf tissue
Mottled streaks running parallel to the midrib, most pronounced on young unfolding leaves
Severe stunting of stools, thin stalks with shortened internodes, and poor tillering
Occasional longitudinal red or necrotic striping on stalks in susceptible cultivars
causes: Transmission by aphid vectors (principally Rhopalosiphum maidis and Melanaphis sacchari) in a non-persistent manner
Use of infected seed cane from previously diseased stools
Mechanical transmission during knife cutting and sett preparation
Presence of collateral hosts including wild grasses, sorghum, and maize around the field perimeter
management: Rogue out and destroy infected young plants along with root systems during first 3 months of planting
Control aphid vector populations using integrated pest management and bio-rational insecticides if vector pressure is high
Clean harvesting tools with 5% trisodium phosphate (TSP) or alcohol disinfectant
prevention: Propagate only tissue-cultured virus-free plantlets or certified nursery setts
Eradicate grassy weeds (such as Sorghum halepense and Digitaria species) surrounding the field
Avoid intercropping or planting adjacent to susceptible sweet sorghum or maize crops
Switch to resistant commercial cultivars
Mosaic.when_to_seek_help: Consult an agricultural extension officer to confirm virus strain if mosaic symptoms appear across more than 5% of your cane nursery.

Yellow.name: Sugarcane Yellow Leaf
Yellow.pathogen: Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Virus (SCYLV) / Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Phytoplasma
Yellow.description: A chronic vascular disease leading to intense yellowing of the central leaf midrib that spreads outward onto the lamina. It disrupts carbohydrate translocation, resulting in reduced juice purity and cane weight.
symptoms: Prominent, bright yellow discoloration along the underside of the midrib on leaves 3 to 6 from top
Discoloration progresses to adjacent lamina tissue, followed by tip necrosis and leaf desiccation
Bunchy top appearance and shortened terminal internodes in advanced stages
Symptoms become most pronounced as cane reaches maturity (6 to 10 months of age)
causes: Primary transmission through the sugarcane aphid (Melanaphis sacchari)
Planting symptomless, chronically infected seed setts
Aggravated by moisture stress, water stagnation, or extreme summer heat
management: Differentiate from nitrogen deficiency or soil salinity (which affects older lower leaves first)
Provide light, frequent irrigation to reduce plant stress during hot dry spells
Manage aphid vector colonies in the cane nursery using recommended neem formulations or IPM sprays
Do not use stalks from symptomatic stools for future planting or ratoon cycles
prevention: Plant virus-tested tissue-culture plantlets or certified seed cane
Adopt hot water treatment (50°C for 2 hours) to suppress phytoplasma transmission
Maintain optimal soil fertility with balanced N, P, K, and micronutrients (especially zinc and iron)
Select varieties showing field tolerance or resistance
Yellow.when_to_seek_help: Because Yellow Leaf symptoms closely resemble nutrient stress and moisture shock, obtain an extension officer's confirmation before making major management decisions.

BacterialBlight.name: Bacterial Blight / Leaf Scald
BacterialBlight.description: A serious bacterial vascular disease that causes diagnostic white 'pencil lines' along leaf veins, followed by severe leaf scalding, inward leaf curling, and side-shooting of stalks.
symptoms: Narrow, well-defined white to yellowish pencil-line streaks along leaf veins running from margin to sheath
Broad necrotic bleaching or scalding of leaf tips, causing leaves to curl inward like a buggy whip
Abnormal sprouting of side shoots (lalas) on mature stalks from the base upwards
Internal vascular reddening in stalk nodal regions with reddish streaks in cross-sections
causes: Primary spread through contaminated cane harvest knives and mechanical harvesters
Infected seed setts harboring systemic bacterial populations
Bacterial exudate washed by rainfall and wind-driven storms into plant wounds and stomata
High humidity coupled with warm temperatures (25°C to 35°C)
management: Rogue and burn stools showing chronic white pencil lines or wilting immediately
Sterilize cutting implements frequently with 1% quaternary ammonium compound or fire flamed
Avoid cutting or handling crops when foliage is wet from rain or dew
Ensure prompt drainage in fields prone to water stagnation
prevention: Plant certified leaf-scald resistant cultivars
Subject seed cane to cold-soak followed by hot-water treatment (cold soak for 24 hours, then 50°C for 3 hours)
Establish dedicated disease-free nurseries away from commercial ratoon fields
Enforce strict farm biosecurity and tool sanitation
BacterialBlight.when_to_seek_help: Notify the local plant health authority immediately if narrow white pencil lines with leaf tip scalding appear in your seed multiplication plot.
